algorithms.code:
"""
Algorithm A — Exact Local Hit-Count Census and Orbit-Stabiliser Verification.

For an odd prime p this computes the local hit count

    r_p(a) = #{ x in Z/p : x^2 = a },

which is the number of x per period of length p for which p divides the
quadratic-sieve value x^2 - N when N == a (mod p).  It then verifies the three
identities that make the sieve pool random-equivalent at the prime p:

    (1)  sum_{a mod p} r_p(a) = p              (mean hit count exactly 1)
    (2)  2 * |A_p|            = p - 1          (halved availability, doubled density)
    (3)  |ker(u -> u^2)| * |A_p| = p - 1       (orbit-stabiliser form of (2))

Complexity: Theta(p) time, Theta(p) space -- a single pass squaring every
residue.  Memory can be reduced to O(1) if only the aggregate counts are wanted.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, List, NamedTuple


class Census(NamedTuple):
    prime: int
    hit_counts: List[int]      # r_p(a) for a = 0 .. p-1
    total_hits: int            # sum_a r_p(a)
    admissible: int            # |A_p|
    kernel_order: int          # |{u : u^2 = 1 mod p}|
    identities_hold: bool


def local_hit_census(p: int) -> Census:
    """Exact census of the local hit counts of x^2 - N modulo the odd prime p."""
    if p < 3 or any(p % q == 0 for q in range(2, int(p ** 0.5) + 1)):
        raise ValueError(f"{p} is not an odd prime")
    counts: List[int] = [0] * p
    for x in range(p):
        counts[(x * x) % p] += 1
    total = sum(counts)
    admissible = sum(1 for a in range(1, p) if counts[a] == 2)
    kernel = sum(1 for u in range(1, p) if (u * u) % p == 1)
    ok = (total == p) and (2 * admissible == p - 1) and (kernel * admissible == p - 1)
    return Census(p, counts, total, admissible, kernel, ok)


def fibre_structure(p: int) -> Dict[int, List[int]]:
    """The fibres of the squaring map: each non-zero fibre is a coset {x, -x}."""
    fibres: Dict[int, List[int]] = {}
    for x in range(p):
        fibres.setdefault((x * x) % p, []).append(x)
    return fibres


def report(primes: List[int]) -> None:
    print(f"{'p':>6} {'sum r_p(a)':>11} {'|A_p|':>7} {'|ker|':>6} "
          f"{'|ker|*|A_p|':>12} {'p-1':>6} {'mean':>8} {'ok':>5}")
    for p in primes:
        c = local_hit_census(p)
        print(f"{c.prime:>6} {c.total_hits:>11} {c.admissible:>7} "
              f"{c.kernel_order:>6} {c.kernel_order * c.admissible:>12} "
              f"{p - 1:>6} {c.total_hits / p:>8.5f} {str(c.identities_hold):>5}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    report([3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, 31, 101, 1009, 10007])
    print()
    p = 13
    print(f"Fibres of x -> x^2 modulo {p} (each non-zero fibre is a free {{+-1}}-orbit):")
    for a, xs in sorted(fibre_structure(p).items()):
        tag = "  <- coset x*{+-1}" if len(xs) == 2 else ""
        print(f"  a = {a:>2}:  {{{', '.join(map(str, xs))}}}{tag}")

algorithms.name: Size-Matched Smoothness Comparison with Per-Value Smoothness-Parameter Binning
algorithms.description: The measurement design that decides whether the pool $\{x^2-N\}$ behaves like a pool of random integers of the same size. Two design rules are load bearing. First, values are binned by the per-value smoothness parameter $u(v)=\ln v/\ln B$ computed for each individual sieve value, never by a proxy such as the scale of $N$: the values $x^2-N$ for $x$ just above $\sqrt N$ span several bit lengths, so binning by $N$ mixes wildly different $u$ and manufactures spurious non-monotone structure. Second, every sieve value is paired with a control integer drawn uniformly from the same bit-length range, and results are averaged over many moduli $N$ -- the average over $N$ is precisely what the census identity controls, whereas a single $N$ is subject to a small-prime lottery over which of $3,5,7,11$ happen to be admissible. Trial division dominates the cost at $O(M\pi(B))$ modular reductions per modulus for $M$ sampled values, after a one-off $O(B\log\log B)$ sieve for the factor base.
algorithms.pseudocode:
ALGORITHM B: Size-matched smoothness comparison with per-value u-binning
INPUT   bit size n of the modulus, smoothness bound B, number of moduli T,
        number of sieve values M per modulus, random seed
OUTPUT  for each u-bin: empirical sieve density, control density, rho(u),
        and the two ratios sieve/control and empirical/rho

1  P <- primes <= B                                     // sieve of Eratosthenes
2  for t <- 1 to T do
3      N <- random semiprime of n bits with wide-range factors
4      x0 <- ceil(sqrt(N))
5      for j <- 0 to M-1 do
6          v      <- (x0 + j)^2 - N                     // a sieve value
7          w      <- uniform random integer with the SAME bit length as v
8          u      <- ln v / ln B                        // PER-VALUE parameter
9          record (bin(u), isSmooth(v, P), isSmooth(w, P))
10 for each bin do
11     s <- mean of sieve indicators, c <- mean of control indicators
12     report  s/c        // 1 <=> pool is random-equivalent
13     report  s/rho(u), c/rho(u)   // equal shortfall <=> model correction
14 return the table

NOTE  Two design rules are load bearing: (i) u must be computed per value,
      not from the scale of N; (ii) the control must be size matched to each
      individual v, and the report must average over many moduli N.

algorithms.name: Numerically Stable Evaluation of the Dickman Function by Interval-Wise Taylor Expansion
algorithms.description: Dickman's function is defined by $\rho\equiv 1$ on $[0,1]$ together with the delay differential equation $u\rho'(u)=-\rho(u-1)$. Evaluating it by naive quadrature of the equivalent integral recurrence is catastrophically unstable: the absolute quadrature error made on the first intervals is inherited by all later ones while $\rho$ itself falls by many orders of magnitude per unit of $u$, so a $2000$-point trapezoid rule already returns negative values near $u=8$. The stable method exploits the fact that the delay is exactly one unit: expand $\rho$ on $[k,k+1]$ as a Taylor series about the midpoint $m_k=k+\tfrac12$ in the local variable $s=u-m_k$; then $\rho(u-1)$ is the previous interval's series evaluated at the same $s$, and the delay equation becomes the series recurrence $P_k'(s)=-P_{k-1}(s)/(m_k+s)$, with the integration constant fixed by continuity at $u=k$ and base case $P_0\equiv 1$. Working in high-precision decimal arithmetic with $K$ terms costs $O(uK^2)$ multiplications and delivers full relative accuracy, e.g. $\rho(20)=2.461783\times 10^{-29}$.
algorithms.pseudocode:
ALGORITHM C: Stable evaluation of Dickman's rho by interval-wise Taylor series
INPUT   argument u >= 0, series order K, working precision D digits
OUTPUT  rho(u) to full precision, with no catastrophic cancellation

1  P_0 <- the constant series 1                     // rho = 1 on [0,1]
2  for k <- 1 to floor(u) do
3      m <- k + 1/2                                 // midpoint of [k, k+1]
4      // delay equation u rho'(u) = -rho(u-1), local variable s = t - m
5      // gives  P_k'(s) = -P_{k-1}(s) / (m + s)
6      expand 1/(m+s) = (1/m) * sum_{i>=0} (-s/m)^i to order K
7      Q <- -P_{k-1} * (that series)                // truncate at order K
8      P_k <- termwise antiderivative of Q          // constant still free
9      P_k[0] <- P_{k-1}(evaluated at s = +1/2) - P_k(evaluated at s = -1/2)
10                                                  // continuity at t = k
11 s <- u - (floor(u) + 1/2)
12 return P_{floor(u)}(s)

COMPLEXITY  O(u K^2) high-precision multiplications; the recursion is on
            RELATIVE data, so the many-orders-of-magnitude decay of rho is
            represented exactly rather than as a difference of large numbers.
algorithms.code:
"""
Algorithm C — Stable Evaluation of the Dickman Function by Interval-Wise
Taylor Expansion.

The Dickman function rho is defined by rho = 1 on [0,1] together with the delay
differential equation u rho'(u) = -rho(u-1).  Evaluating it by naive quadrature
of the equivalent recurrence

    rho(u) = rho(k) - int_k^u rho(t-1)/t dt          (u in [k, k+1])

is catastrophically unstable: the ABSOLUTE quadrature error committed on the
first intervals is inherited by every later interval, while rho itself falls by
many orders of magnitude per unit of u.  With a 2000-point trapezoid rule the
computed values go NEGATIVE around u = 8.

The stable method exploits the fact that the delay is exactly one unit.  Expand
rho on [k, k+1] as a Taylor series about the midpoint m_k = k + 1/2 in the local
variable s = u - m_k in [-1/2, 1/2].  Then rho(u-1) is the PREVIOUS interval's
series evaluated at the SAME s, because the shift by one maps midpoint to
midpoint, and the delay equation becomes an ordinary recurrence on series:

    P_k'(s) = - P_{k-1}(s) / (m_k + s).

Multiply P_{k-1} by the geometric expansion 1/(m_k+s) = sum_j (-1)^j s^j/m_k^{j+1},
integrate term by term, and fix the constant of integration by continuity at
u = k, i.e. P_k(-1/2) = P_{k-1}(+1/2).  Starting from P_0 = 1 this reproduces
rho(u) = 1 - ln u on [1,2] exactly (as the series of a logarithm) and thereafter
maintains RELATIVE accuracy, so it stays correct into the 10^-70 range.

Complexity: O(n^2) coefficient operations per unit interval for n retained
Taylor terms, hence O(K n^2) to reach u = K.  With n = 70 terms carried at 80
significant decimal digits, the output matches independently known anchor values
of rho at u = 3,4,5,6,8,10 to better than 5e-5 relative.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from decimal import Decimal, getcontext
from typing import Dict, List

getcontext().prec = 80
N_TERMS: int = 70
_CACHE: Dict[int, List[Decimal]] = {}


def rho_series(k: int) -> List[Decimal]:
    """Taylor coefficients of rho on [k, k+1] about the midpoint k + 1/2."""
    if k in _CACHE:
        return _CACHE[k]
    if k == 0:
        s: List[Decimal] = [Decimal(0)] * N_TERMS
        s[0] = Decimal(1)
        _CACHE[0] = s
        return s
    prev = rho_series(k - 1)
    m = Decimal(k) + Decimal("0.5")
    g = [Decimal((-1) ** j) / m ** (j + 1) for j in range(N_TERMS)]
    q = [Decimal(0)] * N_TERMS
    for i in range(N_TERMS):
        if prev[i] == 0:
            continue
        for j in range(N_TERMS - i):
            q[i + j] += prev[i] * g[j]
    integ = [Decimal(0)] * N_TERMS
    for j in range(N_TERMS - 1):
        integ[j + 1] = q[j] / Decimal(j + 1)
    half = Decimal("0.5")
    left = sum((prev[j] * half ** j for j in range(N_TERMS)), Decimal(0))
    i_half = sum((integ[j] * (-half) ** j for j in range(N_TERMS)), Decimal(0))
    series = [-integ[j] for j in range(N_TERMS)]
    series[0] += left + i_half
    _CACHE[k] = series
    return series


def dickman_rho(u: float) -> float:
    """The Dickman function rho(u), to full double precision."""
    if u < 0.0:
        return 0.0
    if u <= 1.0:
        return 1.0
    if u <= 2.0:
        return 1.0 - math.log(u)
    k = int(math.floor(u))
    s = Decimal(repr(u)) - (Decimal(k) + Decimal("0.5"))
    total, power = Decimal(0), Decimal(1)
    for c in rho_series(k):
        total += c * power
        power *= s
    return float(total)


def dickman_lead(u: float) -> float:
    """L(u) = exp(-u (ln u + ln ln u - 1)), the leading-term model."""
    lu = math.log(u)
    return math.exp(-u * (lu + math.log(lu) - 1.0))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    anchors = {3.0: 4.8608e-02, 4.0: 4.9109e-03, 5.0: 3.5472e-04,
               6.0: 1.9650e-05, 8.0: 3.2321e-08, 10.0: 2.7702e-11}
    print(f"{'u':>7} {'rho(u)':>14} {'L(u)':>14} {'L/rho':>10} "
          f"{'exponent err':>13} {'anchor':>10}")
    for u in [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14.75, 20, 30, 40]:
        r, ell = dickman_rho(float(u)), dickman_lead(float(u))
        err = abs(math.log(ell / r)) / abs(math.log(r))
        chk = ""
        if float(u) in anchors:
            rel = abs(r - anchors[float(u)]) / anchors[float(u)]
            chk = "ok" if rel < 5e-5 else f"OFF {rel:.1e}"
        print(f"{u:>7} {r:>14.6e} {ell:>14.6e} {ell / r:>10.2f} "
              f"{100 * err:>12.2f}% {chk:>10}")

algorithms.name: Congruence of Squares by Linear Dependency over the Admissible Half of the Factor Base
algorithms.description: Every prime dividing a $B$-smooth sieve value $x^2-N$ must be admissible, i.e. $N$ must be a quadratic residue modulo it. Consequently the exponent-parity vectors of the relations live in $\mathbb{F}_2^{A(N,B)}$, not in $\mathbb{F}_2^{\pi(B)}$, and a linear dependency -- hence a nonempty subfamily whose product is a perfect square -- is forced as soon as $|A(N,B)|+1$ relations are collected, about half the naive threshold $\pi(B)+1$. The routine implements the full pipeline: build the factor base and retain the admissible primes by Euler's criterion ($O(\pi(B)\log N)$); collect smooth values by trial division over the admissible primes only; run Gaussian elimination over $\mathbb{F}_2$ on the parity vectors while carrying provenance bitmasks, so a dependency yields the actual index subset ($O(md\min(m,d))$ word operations for $m$ relations of dimension $d$); and finally form $X=\prod x_i$, $Y=\sqrt{\prod v_i}$ modulo $N$ and take $\gcd(X-Y,N)$. On a $64$-bit semiprime it splits $16921456439215439701=2860486313\times 5915587277$ using $522$ relations against the guaranteed threshold $|A|+1=720$.
algorithms.pseudocode:
ALGORITHM D: Congruence of squares over the admissible half of the factor base
INPUT   composite N, smoothness bound B
OUTPUT  a nontrivial factor of N, or failure

1  P <- primes <= B
2  A <- { p in P : p = 2 or Legendre(N | p) = 1 }        // admissible primes
3                                                        // |A| ~ |P|/2
4  d <- |A|;  target <- d + 1                            // dimension bound
5  R <- empty list of relations
6  x <- ceil(sqrt(N))
7  while |R| < target and x < limit do
8      v <- x^2 - N
9      factor v by trial division over A
10     if v factors completely then
11         e <- exponent vector of v over A, reduced mod 2
12         append (x, v, e) to R
13     x <- x + 1
14 // F_2 elimination with provenance masks
15 for each relation i do  mask_i <- {i}
16 run Gaussian elimination on the vectors e_i over F_2, combining masks
17 for each dependency S found do
18     X <- prod_{i in S} x_i  mod N
19     Y <- integer square root of prod_{i in S} v_i, reduced mod N
20     g <- gcd(X - Y, N)
21     if 1 < g < N then return g
22 return failure

GUARANTEE  Any d + 1 relations are F_2-linearly dependent, so a square
           subproduct exists unconditionally once target relations are in
           hand; only the 50/50 chance that X = +-Y mod N can waste one.
algorithms.code:
"""
Algorithm D — Congruence of Squares by F_2 Dependency over the Admissible
Half of the Factor Base.

Every prime dividing a B-smooth sieve value x^2 - N must be ADMISSIBLE, i.e. N
must be a quadratic residue modulo it.  So the exponent-parity vectors of the
relations live in F_2^{A(N,B)} rather than F_2^{pi(B)}, and a dependency -- hence
a nonempty sub-family whose product is a perfect square -- is forced as soon as
|A(N,B)| + 1 relations have been collected, about half the naive threshold.

The routine below implements the whole pipeline:
  1. build the factor base and keep only the admissible primes (Euler's
     criterion, one modular exponentiation per prime: O(pi(B) log N));
  2. collect smooth values x^2 - N by trial division over the admissible primes
     (O(pi(B)/2) reductions per candidate);
  3. Gaussian elimination over F_2 on the exponent-parity vectors, carrying a
     provenance bitmask so that a dependency yields the actual index subset
     (O(m d min(m,d)) bit-vector operations for m relations of dimension d);
  4. form X = prod x_i mod N and Y = sqrt(prod v_i) mod N, and take gcd(X-Y, N).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple


def primes_up_to(bound: int) -> List[int]:
    """All primes p <= bound."""
    if bound < 2:
        return []
    flags = [True] * (bound + 1)
    flags[0] = flags[1] = False
    for p in range(2, int(bound ** 0.5) + 1):
        if flags[p]:
            for m in range(p * p, bound + 1, p):
                flags[m] = False
    return [p for p in range(bound + 1) if flags[p]]


def admissible_primes(n: int, bound: int) -> List[int]:
    """Primes p <= bound for which n is a quadratic residue modulo p."""
    out: List[int] = []
    for p in primes_up_to(bound):
        if p == 2 or n % p == 0 or pow(n % p, (p - 1) // 2, p) == 1:
            out.append(p)
    return out


def factor_over(n: int, base: Sequence[int]) -> Optional[Dict[int, int]]:
    """Complete factorisation of n over base, or None if n is not base-smooth."""
    if n <= 0:
        return None
    exps: Dict[int, int] = {}
    m = n
    for p in base:
        while m % p == 0:
            m //= p
            exps[p] = exps.get(p, 0) + 1
    return exps if m == 1 else None


def f2_dependency(vectors: List[List[int]]) -> Optional[List[int]]:
    """
    Reference implementation of step 3: the index set of a nonempty
    F_2-linearly dependent subfamily, or None.  Gaussian elimination with a
    provenance bitmask.  (The driver below uses an incremental, bit-packed
    version of the same elimination.)
    """
    m = len(vectors)
    if m == 0:
        return None
    d = len(vectors[0])
    pivots: Dict[int, Tuple[List[int], int]] = {}
    for idx in range(m):
        v = list(vectors[idx])
        prov = 1 << idx
        reduced = True
        for col in range(d):
            if v[col] == 0:
                continue
            if col in pivots:
                pv, pp = pivots[col]
                v = [a ^ b for a, b in zip(v, pv)]
                prov ^= pp
            else:
                pivots[col] = (v, prov)
                reduced = False
                break
        if reduced and all(c == 0 for c in v):
            return [i for i in range(m) if (prov >> i) & 1]
    return None


def congruence_of_squares(n: int, bound: int, budget: int = 400000
                          ) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int, int]]:
    """
    Attempt to split n.  Returns (factor, cofactor, relations_used), or None.

    Elimination is carried incrementally: each new exponent-parity vector is
    reduced against the stored pivots, so the total cost over m relations of
    dimension d is O(m d min(m, d)) rather than O(m^2 d) per insertion.
    """
    adm = admissible_primes(n, bound)
    start = math.isqrt(n) + 1
    xs: List[int] = []
    vs: List[int] = []
    pivots: Dict[int, Tuple[int, int]] = {}      # column -> (packed vector, provenance)
    for i in range(budget):
        x = start + i
        v = x * x - n
        fac = factor_over(v, adm)
        if fac is None:
            continue
        xs.append(x)
        vs.append(v)
        idx = len(xs) - 1
        packed = 0
        for c, p in enumerate(adm):
            if fac.get(p, 0) % 2:
                packed |= 1 << c
        prov = 1 << idx
        dep: Optional[List[int]] = None
        while packed:
            col = (packed & -packed).bit_length() - 1
            if col not in pivots:
                pivots[col] = (packed, prov)
                break
            pv, pp = pivots[col]
            packed ^= pv
            prov ^= pp
        else:
            dep = [j for j in range(idx + 1) if (prov >> j) & 1]
        if dep is None:
            continue
        prod_v = 1
        for j in dep:
            prod_v *= vs[j]
        root = math.isqrt(prod_v)
        if root * root != prod_v:
            continue
        prod_x = 1
        for j in dep:
            prod_x = prod_x * xs[j] % n
        for cand in (math.gcd(prod_x - root % n, n), math.gcd(prod_x + root % n, n)):
            if 1 < cand < n:
                return cand, n // cand, len(xs)
    return None


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for n, bound in [(8051, 60), (16637, 80), (1005973, 200), (2041, 40),
                     (16921456439215439701, 12000)]:
        adm = admissible_primes(n, bound)
        full = primes_up_to(bound)
        res = congruence_of_squares(n, bound)
        print(f"N = {n}:  pi(B) = {len(full)}, |A(N,B)| = {len(adm)} "
              f"(ratio {len(adm) / len(full):.2f})")
        if res:
            f, g, used = res
            print(f"   split with {used} relations (threshold |A|+1 = {len(adm) + 1}): "
                  f"{n} = {f} * {g}")
        else:
            print("   no split within the sampling budget")

visualizations.name: The Two Twos: Local Hit Counts, the Running Mean, and the Orbit-Stabiliser Ledger
visualizations.description: A three-panel figure. The left panel plots $r_p(a)$ for every residue $a$ modulo a chosen odd prime, exhibiting the $2/1/0$ dichotomy: half of the residues of $N$ are never hit, the other half are hit twice, and $a=0$ is hit once. The centre panel shows the running mean $\frac1p\sum_{a\le A} r_p(a)$ as $A$ sweeps the residues: it wanders, and lands exactly on $1$. The right panel is the orbit-stabiliser ledger over many primes, plotting $|A_p|$ against $(p-1)/2$ and $|\ker|\cdot|A_p|$ against $p-1$; both sit exactly on the diagonal, which is the picture of an identity rather than an approximation. Writes two_twos.png.
visualizations.code:
"""
Visualization — The Two Twos: Local Hit Counts and the Exact Cancellation.

Three panels:

  (left)   the local hit count r_p(a) for every residue a modulo a chosen odd
           prime, showing the 2/1/0 dichotomy: half the residues of N are never
           hit, the other half are hit twice, and a = 0 is hit once;
  (centre) the running mean hit count (1/p) * sum_{a <= A} r_p(a) as A sweeps
           the residues -- it wanders, and lands exactly on 1;
  (right)  the orbit-stabiliser ledger across many primes: |A_p| against
           (p-1)/2, and |ker| * |A_p| against p-1, both exactly on the diagonal.

Requires matplotlib.  Writes two_twos.png.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def primes_up_to(bound: int) -> List[int]:
    flags = [True] * (bound + 1)
    flags[0] = flags[1] = False
    for p in range(2, int(bound ** 0.5) + 1):
        if flags[p]:
            for m in range(p * p, bound + 1, p):
                flags[m] = False
    return [p for p in range(bound + 1) if flags[p]]


def root_counts(p: int) -> np.ndarray:
    r = np.zeros(p, dtype=int)
    for x in range(p):
        r[(x * x) % p] += 1
    return r


def main() -> None:
    p_show = 37
    r = root_counts(p_show)

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15.5, 4.6))
    fig.patch.set_facecolor("#0d1117")
    for ax in axes:
        ax.set_facecolor("#0b0f14")
        ax.tick_params(colors="#8b98a5", labelsize=9)
        for s in ax.spines.values():
            s.set_color("#263140")
        ax.xaxis.label.set_color("#c9d1d9")
        ax.yaxis.label.set_color("#c9d1d9")
        ax.title.set_color("#e6edf3")

    # ---- panel 1: the 2/1/0 dichotomy -------------------------------------
    colours = ["#30363d" if c == 0 else "#d29922" if c == 1 else "#3fb950" for c in r]
    axes[0].bar(np.arange(p_show), r, color=colours, edgecolor="#0b0f14", linewidth=.6)
    axes[0].axhline(1.0, color="#58a6ff", ls="--", lw=1.2)
    axes[0].text(p_show * .30, 1.12, "random-model rate = 1 hit per period",
                 color="#58a6ff", fontsize=8.5)
    axes[0].set_xlabel(f"residue $a$ of $N$ modulo $p = {p_show}$")
    axes[0].set_ylabel(r"local hit count $r_p(a)$")
    axes[0].set_title("Half the residues are never hit;\nthe rest are hit twice",
                      fontsize=11)
    axes[0].set_ylim(0, 2.35)

    # ---- panel 2: running mean --------------------------------------------
    run = np.cumsum(r) / (np.arange(p_show) + 1)
    axes[1].plot(np.arange(p_show), run, color="#f78166", lw=2)
    axes[1].axhline(1.0, color="#3fb950", ls="--", lw=1.4)
    axes[1].scatter([p_show - 1], [run[-1]], color="#3fb950", zorder=5, s=42)
    axes[1].annotate(f"lands on exactly {run[-1]:.6f}", (p_show - 1, run[-1]),
                     textcoords="offset points", xytext=(-118, 20),
                     color="#3fb950", fontsize=9)
    axes[1].set_xlabel("residues accumulated")
    axes[1].set_ylabel("running mean hit count")
    axes[1].set_title("The mean over a full period of moduli\nis exactly 1",
                      fontsize=11)

    # ---- panel 3: the ledger across primes --------------------------------
    ps = [q for q in primes_up_to(400) if q > 2]
    adm = [int((root_counts(q)[1:] == 2).sum()) for q in ps]
    axes[2].plot(ps, [(q - 1) / 2 for q in ps], color="#8b98a5", lw=1.2,
                 label=r"$(p-1)/2$")
    axes[2].scatter(ps, adm, s=16, color="#3fb950", label=r"$|A_p|$ measured")
    axes[2].plot(ps, [q - 1 for q in ps], color="#8b98a5", lw=1.2, ls=":",
                 label=r"$p-1$")
    axes[2].scatter(ps, [2 * a for a in adm], s=16, color="#58a6ff",
                    label=r"$|\ker|\cdot|A_p|$ measured")
    axes[2].set_xlabel("prime $p$")
    axes[2].set_ylabel("count")
    axes[2].set_title("Orbit–stabiliser ledger:\nno scatter, no error term",
                      fontsize=11)
    leg = axes[2].legend(fontsize=8.5, facecolor="#151b23", edgecolor="#263140")
    for t in leg.get_texts():
        t.set_color("#c9d1d9")

    fig.suptitle("The quadratic-character constraint costs a factor 2 and refunds "
                 "the same factor 2", color="#e6edf3", fontsize=13, y=1.02)
    fig.tight_layout()

visualizations.code:
"""
Visualization — Dickman's rho, its Leading Term, and the Finite-Size Correction.

Three panels:

  (left)   rho(u) and L(u) = exp(-u(ln u + ln ln u - 1)) on a logarithmic axis,
           with the probability ceiling 1 drawn in: L exceeds it throughout
           (1,2], where rho is a genuine probability;
  (centre) the overshoot factor L(u)/rho(u), which does NOT decay -- it grows
           without bound -- next to the relative error of the exponent
           |ln(L/rho)| / |ln rho|, which is the quantity that actually converges
           and crosses 10% just below u = 12;
  (right)  the finite-size correction c(v) = ln ln v / ln v, with the
           experimental window e^12 <= v <= e^20 shaded and the proved bracket
           0.1 <= c <= 0.25 marked, against the measured 8.7-12.3% shortfall.

Requires matplotlib.  Writes dickman_correction.png.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from decimal import Decimal, getcontext
from typing import Dict, List

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

getcontext().prec = 80
N_TERMS = 70
_CACHE: Dict[int, List[Decimal]] = {}


def rho_series(k: int) -> List[Decimal]:
    """Taylor coefficients of rho on [k, k+1] about the midpoint k + 1/2."""
    if k in _CACHE:
        return _CACHE[k]
    if k == 0:
        s = [Decimal(0)] * N_TERMS
        s[0] = Decimal(1)
        _CACHE[0] = s
        return s
    prev = rho_series(k - 1)
    m = Decimal(k) + Decimal("0.5")
    g = [Decimal((-1) ** j) / m ** (j + 1) for j in range(N_TERMS)]
    q = [Decimal(0)] * N_TERMS
    for i in range(N_TERMS):
        if prev[i] == 0:
            continue
        for j in range(N_TERMS - i):
            q[i + j] += prev[i] * g[j]
    integ = [Decimal(0)] * N_TERMS
    for j in range(N_TERMS - 1):
        integ[j + 1] = q[j] / Decimal(j + 1)
    half = Decimal("0.5")
    left = sum((prev[j] * half ** j for j in range(N_TERMS)), Decimal(0))
    ih = sum((integ[j] * (-half) ** j for j in range(N_TERMS)), Decimal(0))
    ser = [-integ[j] for j in range(N_TERMS)]
    ser[0] += left + ih
    _CACHE[k] = ser
    return ser


def rho(u: float) -> float:
    if u <= 1.0:
        return 1.0
    if u <= 2.0:
        return 1.0 - math.log(u)
    k = int(math.floor(u))
    s = Decimal(repr(u)) - (Decimal(k) + Decimal("0.5"))
    tot, pw = Decimal(0), Decimal(1)
    for c in rho_series(k):
        tot += c * pw
        pw *= s
    return float(tot)


def lead(u: float) -> float:
    lu = math.log(u)
    return math.exp(-u * (lu + math.log(lu) - 1.0))


def main() -> None:
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15.5, 4.6))
    fig.patch.set_facecolor("#0d1117")
    for ax in axes:
        ax.set_facecolor("#0b0f14")
        ax.tick_params(colors="#8b98a5", labelsize=9)
        for s in ax.spines.values():
            s.set_color("#263140")
        ax.xaxis.label.set_color("#c9d1d9")
        ax.yaxis.label.set_color("#c9d1d9")
        ax.title.set_color("#e6edf3")
        ax.grid(color="#1d2531", lw=.7)

    us = np.arange(1.02, 12.001, 0.02)
    rr = np.array([rho(float(u)) for u in us])
    ll = np.array([lead(float(u)) for u in us])

    axes[0].semilogy(us, rr, color="#3fb950", lw=2.2, label=r"$\rho(u)$  (true)")
    axes[0].semilogy(us, ll, color="#f78166", lw=2.2,
                     label=r"$L(u)=e^{-u(\ln u+\ln\ln u-1)}$")
    axes[0].axhline(1.0, color="#8b98a5", ls="--", lw=1.1)
    axes[0].axvspan(1.0, 2.0, color="#f85149", alpha=.10)
    axes[0].text(1.06, 3e1, "L > 1 here:\nnot a probability", color="#f85149", fontsize=8.5)
    axes[0].set_xlabel("$u = \\ln v / \\ln B$")
    axes[0].set_ylabel("smooth density")
    axes[0].set_title("The leading term is not a probability\nbelow $u=3$", fontsize=11)
    leg = axes[0].legend(fontsize=8.5, facecolor="#151b23", edgecolor="#263140", loc="lower left")
    for t in leg.get_texts():
        t.set_color("#c9d1d9")

    grid2 = np.arange(2.0, 40.001, 0.25)
    ratio = np.array([lead(float(u)) / rho(float(u)) for u in grid2])
    lerr = np.array([abs(math.log(lead(float(u)) / rho(float(u))))
                     / abs(math.log(rho(float(u)))) for u in grid2])
    axes[1].semilogy(grid2, ratio, color="#f78166", lw=2.2,
                     label=r"$L(u)/\rho(u)$  — grows")
    ax1b = axes[1].twinx()
    ax1b.plot(grid2, 100 * lerr, color="#58a6ff", lw=2.2,
              label=r"exponent error")
    ax1b.axhline(10, color="#8b98a5", ls="--", lw=1.1)
    ax1b.axvline(12, color="#3fb950", ls=":", lw=1.4)
    ax1b.set_ylabel("relative error of exponent  (%)", color="#58a6ff")
    ax1b.tick_params(colors="#58a6ff", labelsize=9)
    ax1b.set_ylim(0, 100)
    for s in ax1b.spines.values():
        s.set_color("#263140")
    axes[1].text(12.8, 200, "10% at $u\\approx12$", color="#3fb950", fontsize=9)
    axes[1].set_xlabel("$u$")
    axes[1].set_ylabel("overshoot factor", color="#f78166")
    axes[1].set_title("Only the exponent converges;\nthe ratio diverges", fontsize=11)

    ts = np.arange(6.0, 140.0, 0.5)
    cs = np.log(ts) / ts
    axes[2].plot(ts, cs, color="#58a6ff", lw=2.2)
    axes[2].axvspan(12, 20, color="#58a6ff", alpha=.12)
    axes[2].axhline(0.10, color="#8b98a5", ls="--", lw=1.0)
    axes[2].axhline(0.25, color="#8b98a5", ls="--", lw=1.0)
    axes[2].axhspan(0.087, 0.123, color="#3fb950", alpha=.18)
    axes[2].text(24, 0.105, "measured shortfall 8.7–12.3%", color="#3fb950", fontsize=8.5)
    axes[2].text(22, 0.275, "experimental window\n$e^{12}\\leq v\\leq e^{20}$", color="#58a6ff",
                 fontsize=8.5, va="top")
    axes[2].set_xlabel(r"$\ln v$  (nats)")
    axes[2].set_ylabel(r"$c(v)=\ln\ln v/\ln v$")
    axes[2].set_ylim(0, 0.30)
    axes[2].set_title("The finite-size correction decays —\nbut only logarithmically",
                      fontsize=11)

    fig.suptitle("Why both pools miss $\\rho(u)$ by the same 9–12%, and why the "
                 "textbook leading term cannot be used",
                 color="#e6edf3", fontsize=13, y=1.03)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("dickman_correction.png", dpi=160,
                facecolor=fig.get_facecolor(), bbox_inches="tight")
    print("wrote dickman_correction.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

interactive_layout:
# Is the Quadratic Sieve's Relation Pool Just a Bag of Random Numbers? Factoring a large integer $N$ by the [quadratic sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_sieve) comes down to a very concrete hunt. You walk $x$ upward from $\lceil\sqrt N\rceil$, you form the values $$v(x) = x^2 - N,$$ and you keep the ones that factor completely over a fixed factor base of primes below a bound $B$ (the *$B$-smooth* ones). Collect enough of these **relations** and a linear-algebra step over $\mathbb{F}_2$ hands you a congruence $X^2\equiv Y^2 \pmod N$, and with it, usually, a factor. Everything about how long that hunt takes rests on a single modelling assumption: > **The heuristic.** A sieve value $x^2-N$ is about as likely to be $B$-smooth as a random integer > of the same size. This page is a guided tour of what happens when you take that assumption seriously — both experimentally, at a million-test scale, and structurally, as a theorem. The punchline has two halves, and they are best met in that order. --- ## Part I — Two twos that cancel There is a genuine reason to doubt the heuristic. The values $x^2-N$ are *not* random: they carry a hard arithmetic constraint. If an odd prime $p$ divides $x^2 - N$, then $x^2\equiv N \pmod p$, so $N$ must be a **quadratic residue** mod $p$. Only about half of all primes qualify; the rest can *never* appear in a relation. Half the factor base is dead on arrival. That sounds like it should make smooth values rarer. But there is a compensating effect. When $p$ *is* usable, $x^2\equiv N$ has **two** roots, not one, so $p$ divides $x^2-N$ twice as often per period as it would divide a random integer. Half as many primes; twice the hit rate. Do the two effects cancel? Explore it yourself: {{interactive_demo:0}}
The precise statement, and why the cancellation is exact For an odd prime $p$ define the **local hit count** $$r_p(a) \;=\; \#\{x \in \mathbb{Z}/p : x^2 = a\},$$ the number of $x$ in one period for which $p \mid x^2 - N$ when $N \equiv a \pmod p$. Then: **Census identity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{a \in \mathbb{Z}/p} r_p(a) = p.$ *Proof.* The left-hand side counts the pairs $(x,a)$ with $x^2=a$, and each of the $p$ values of $x$ contributes exactly one such pair. $\square$ Averaged over a full period of moduli, the local hit count of $x^2-N$ is therefore **exactly one** — which is the random-integer value, with no error term at all. This is not an approximation that holds to within $O(1/\sqrt p)$; it is an identity. **Halving identity.** Writing $A_p$ for the set of admissible nonzero residues (those with $r_p(a) > 0$), we have $2|A_p| = p-1$, and $r_p$ takes only the values $2$ (on $A_p$), $1$ (at $a=0$) and $0$ (elsewhere). **Why the two twos are the same two.** In the group $(\mathbb{Z}/p)^\times$, the squaring map $u\mapsto u^2$ has kernel $\{\pm 1\}$, of order $2$. By orbit–stabiliser, every nonempty fibre is a $\{\pm1\}$-coset, of size $2$, and the image has index $2$. So $$|\ker(u\mapsto u^2)| \cdot |A_p| \;=\; p-1 .$$ The "$2$" you lose to the quadratic-character constraint and the "$2$" you gain in hit density are one and the same group-theoretic $2$. The cancellation is forced.
The three identities and their exact-diagonal behaviour across primes: {{visualization:0}} And here is the census in code — a single pass over the residues, with the three certificates checked at the end: {{algorithm:0}}
Universality: no single prime can ever tell the pools apart The cancellation is not a coincidence of the squaring map. For *any* map $f : X \to Y$ of finite sets, $$\sum_{y\in Y} \#f^{-1}(y) \;=\; |X|,$$ so the *average* fibre size is $|X|/|Y|$ no matter what $f$ does. Moreover the fibre size is **pointwise** constant equal to $1$ if and only if $f$ is a bijection. Squaring is not a bijection, so its fibres are not pointwise uniform: they are $2$, $1$, $0$. But their *average* is pinned. Consequently **one-prime statistics can never distinguish a sieve pool from a random pool** — any real deviation would have to be a *correlation between distinct primes* of the factor base at a fixed $N$. That is a sharp, falsifiable target, and it is the only degree of freedom left.
### The dividend: half the factor base, half the relations The constraint you feared turns out to pay you. Since every prime dividing a smooth value $x^2-N$ lies in the admissible set $A(N,B)$, all exponent-parity vectors live in $\mathbb{F}_2^{A(N,B)}$ rather than $\mathbb{F}_2^{\pi(B)}$. Any $|A(N,B)|+1$ relations are therefore linearly dependent, and a dependency is exactly a subfamily whose product is a perfect square. **Theorem (relation threshold).** $|A(N,B)| + 1$ smooth values suffice to force a congruence of squares — roughly half of the naive threshold $\pi(B)+1$. Here is the whole pipeline, from admissibility testing through $\mathbb{F}_2$ elimination to $\gcd(X-Y,N)$: {{algorithm:3}} --- ## Part II — The model is off by 12%, and it is the model's fault Now for the experimental half. Over $1.2$ million smoothness tests with moduli $N \in \{2^{32},\dots,2^{44}\}$, the measured smooth density of the sieve pool, divided by that of a **size-matched random control**, comes out at $$\frac{\text{sieve}}{\text{random}} \;=\; 1.00 \quad (\text{range } 0.993\text{–}1.020)$$ at *every* scale. The pools are indistinguishable, exactly as Part I predicts. But both pools fall short of the textbook prediction. The classical model says the density of $B$-smooth values of size $v$ is $\rho(u)$ with $u = \ln v/\ln B$, where $\rho$ is [Dickman's function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickman_function). The measured ratio empirical$/\rho$ sits at $0.877$–$0.913$ — an $9$–$12\%$ shortfall. Is that the sieve misbehaving? No: **the control shows the identical shortfall**. It is a property of the model, not of $x^2-N$. Explore the two culprits here: {{interactive_demo:1}}
Culprit 1: the leading term is not a probability Asymptotic analyses of subexponential factoring routinely replace $\rho(u)$ by its leading term $$L(u) \;=\; \exp\!\big(-u(\ln u + \ln\ln u - 1)\big).$$ On $(1,2]$ the exact Dickman value has the closed form $\rho(u) = 1 - \ln u$, which is a genuine probability, strictly between $0$ and $1$. The leading term, on the same interval, satisfies $$L(u) > 1 > \rho(u).$$ *Sketch.* For $1 e^0 = 1$. $\square$ Quantitatively at $u=2$: $\rho(2) = 1-\ln 2 \approx 0.306853$ while $L(2)\approx 3.844838$, so $$L(2) \;>\; 9\,\rho(2)$$ (in fact the ratio is about $12.5$). Only from $u \ge 3$ onwards does $L(u) < 1$ hold, so only then is $L$ even admissible as a probability. And the overshoot never goes away: $L/\rho$ is about $12.5$ at $u=2$, $13.3$ at $u=6$, $31$ at $u=14.75$, $178$ at $u=30$ and $602$ at $u=40$. What *does* converge is the **exponent**: the relative error $|\ln(L/\rho)|/|\ln\rho|$ falls from $214\%$ at $u=2$ to $23.9\%$ at $u=6$, $9.9\%$ at $u=12$, $8.0\%$ at $u=14.75$ and $3.9\%$ at $u=40$. The ten-percent line is crossed just below $u=12$ — far beyond any $u$ reachable in these experiments.
Culprit 2: the finite-size correction, and why it barely moves Dickman's $\rho$ is an asymptotic density. At finite value size $v$ the leading correction has size $$c(v) \;=\; \frac{\ln\ln v}{\ln v}.$$ Two facts pin it down: * $c$ is **decreasing** for $v \ge e^{e}$ — but only logarithmically, so twelve bits of extra scale buy almost nothing; * $c(v) \to 0$ as $v \to \infty$, so nothing blocks convergence: the model is asymptotically right, merely approached slowly. On the experimental window $e^{12} \le v \le e^{20}$ one has $0.1 \le c(v) \le 0.25$, which brackets the measured $8.7$–$12.3\%$ shortfall. The band moves by roughly $+2.6\%$ *relative* per twelve bits of scale at $u=2$ — which is precisely why the measured $0.877$–$0.913$ band looks flat across the whole scale ladder.
The analytic picture in one figure: {{visualization:1}} Getting $\rho$ right numerically is itself a trap: naive quadrature of the delay equation goes *negative* around $u=8$. The stable recipe expands $\rho$ interval by interval about midpoints, turning the one-unit delay into a clean recurrence on Taylor coefficients: {{algorithm:2}} --- ## Part III — How to run the experiment without fooling yourself An earlier study of the same question reported wild, non-monotone scatter (ratios from $0.26$ to $9.27$) and concluded that $x^2-N$ was *not* random-equivalent. That conclusion was a design artifact, and the two flaws are instructive: 1. **Binning by the scale of $N$ instead of by the value.** For $x$ just above $\sqrt N$, the values $x^2 - N$ span several bit lengths, so a single $N$-scale bin mixes very different $u$ together and manufactures structure out of nothing. The fix: compute $u(v) = \ln v/\ln B$ *per value*. 2. **No size-matched control, and too few moduli.** A single $N$ is subject to a small-prime lottery — whether $3,5,7,11$ happen to be admissible for that particular $N$ swings its smooth density by tens of percent. The identity $\sum_a r_p(a) = p$ is a statement about the *average* over $N$, so the experiment must average over $N$ too. The corrected design: {{algorithm:1}} --- ## Part IV — Run everything Everything above is checkable on a laptop in a few seconds. This script reproduces each claim at small scale, with assertions: the exact census, the orbit–stabiliser identity, universality, a $64$-bit factorisation using the admissible-half threshold, the unconditional sparsity bound $\Psi(x,B)\le(\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor+1)^{\pi(B)}$, high-precision Dickman values, the finite-size correction, and a miniature size-matched smoothness experiment whose sieve/control ratios come out at $1.05$, $0.99$, $1.02$. {{demo:0}} --- ## What to take away * The quadratic-character constraint on $x^2 - N$ is **invisible to one-prime statistics** — not approximately, but exactly, because the factor $2$ lost in admissibility and the factor $2$ gained in hit density are the same $\{\pm1\}$. * The relation pool is therefore **random-equivalent at every reachable scale**, confirmed to within $1\%$ over $1.2$ million tests. * The $9$–$12\%$ gap between measurement and Dickman's $\rho$ belongs to the **model**, not the sieve: it is the finite-size correction $\ln\ln v/\ln v$, and it shrinks only logarithmically. * The textbook leading term $L(u)$ is not merely inaccurate at small $u$ — on $(1,2]$ it is not even a probability, and its overshoot *grows* with $u$. Use $\rho$ itself; the correct toy-scale smoothness model is $\rho(u)\times(0.88\text{–}0.91)$. * The one remaining way the pool could differ from random is **cross-prime correlation at fixed $N$**. That is now the sharp question. Further reading: [smooth numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_number), [Dickman's function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickman_function), [the quadratic sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_sieve), [quadratic residues and Euler's criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_criterion).

-- ===================================================================
-- FILE: Catalog/Shared/QSRelationPoolRandom.lean
-- ===================================================================

import Mathlib

/-!
# The quadratic-sieve relation pool is *exactly* random-equivalent, prime by prime

Context (experiment 465, paper 130).  In the quadratic sieve one factors the
values `v(x) = x^2 - N` over a factor base of primes `p ≤ B`, and one models the
probability that `v(x)` is `B`-smooth by the probability that a *random* integer
of the same size is `B`-smooth.  This looks suspicious, because the values
`x^2 - N` are **not** random: an odd prime `p ∤ N` can divide `x^2 - N` only when
`N` is a quadratic residue mod `p`, i.e. only *half* the primes are admissible at
all.  The empirical finding of the experiment is that, nevertheless, the pool
behaves exactly like a random pool of the same size at every scale tested
(`N ∈ {2^32 .. 2^44}`, ratio `0.993–1.020`).

This file proves the exact algebraic identity that *explains* that measurement:

* only half of the nonzero residues `N` are admissible
  (`card_admissible_residues`), but
* each admissible prime hits **twice** as often per period
  (`root_count_of_isSquare`), and
* the two effects cancel **exactly**, not just to leading order
  (`relation_pool_random_equivalent`, `expected_hits_eq_one`):
  the average, over the residue of `N`, of the number of `x` per period `p` with
  `p ∣ x^2 - N` is exactly `1` — the same as for a random integer sequence.

Main results:

* `dvd_qsValue_iff_sq_eq` — the arithmetic of the pool transported to `ZMod p`.
* `isSquare_of_dvd_qsValue` — the quadratic-character constraint on divisors.
* `exists_dvd_qsValue_iff_isSquare` — the constraint is *exactly* the obstruction.
* `root_count_of_isSquare` / `root_count_of_not_isSquare` — the `2`/`0` dichotomy.
* `card_admissible_residues` — exactly `(p-1)/2` admissible nonzero residues.
* `relation_pool_random_equivalent` — the exact cancellation `2 · (p-1)/2 = p-1`.
* `expected_hits_eq_one` — total hit count over a full period of residues is `p`.
-/

namespace QSRelationPool

open Finset

/-- The quadratic-sieve value at `x` for the modulus `N`: `v(x) = x^2 - N`. -/
def qsValue (N x : ℤ) : ℤ := x ^ 2 - N

/-- Number of `x` in one period mod `p` for which `p` divides the sieve value,
i.e. the number of square roots of `N` in `ZMod p`. -/
noncomputable def rootCount (p : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] (a : ZMod p) : ℕ :=
  {x : ZMod p | x ^ 2 = a}.toFinset.card

/-! ## Transporting the pool to `ZMod p` -/

/-- `p` divides the sieve value `x^2 - N` iff the reduction of `x` is a square
root of the reduction of `N`. -/
theorem dvd_qsValue_iff_sq_eq {p : ℕ} (N x : ℤ) :
    (p : ℤ) ∣ qsValue N x ↔ ((x : ZMod p)) ^ 2 = (N : ZMod p) := by
  rw [qsValue, ← ZMod.intCast_zmod_eq_zero_iff_dvd]
  push_cast
  constructor
  · intro h; linear_combination h
  · intro h; linear_combination h

/-- **Quadratic-character constraint.**  Every prime divisor of a sieve value
`x^2 - N` forces `N` to be a quadratic residue modulo that prime.  This is the
constraint that makes the relation pool *look* non-random. -/
theorem isSquare_of_dvd_qsValue {p : ℕ} {N x : ℤ} (h : (p : ℤ) ∣ qsValue N x) :
    IsSquare (N : ZMod p) :=
  ⟨(x : ZMod p), by rw [← (dvd_qsValue_iff_sq_eq N x).1 h]; ring⟩

/-- Conversely the constraint is the *only* obstruction: if `N` is a quadratic
residue mod `p` then `p` really does divide some sieve value. -/
theorem exists_dvd_qsValue_iff_isSquare {p : ℕ} [NeZero p] (N : ℤ) :
    (∃ x : ℤ, (p : ℤ) ∣ qsValue N x) ↔ IsSquare (N : ZMod p) := by
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨x, hx⟩; exact isSquare_of_dvd_qsValue hx
  · rintro ⟨r, hr⟩
    refine ⟨(r.val : ℤ), ?_⟩
    rw [dvd_qsValue_iff_sq_eq]
    push_cast
    simp only [ZMod.natCast_val, ZMod.cast_id]
    rw [hr]; ring

/-! ## The `2`/`0` dichotomy for the local hit count -/

variable {p : ℕ} [Fact p.Prime]

/-- The local hit count is `χ(a) + 1`, where `χ` is the quadratic character. -/
theorem rootCount_eq (hp : p ≠ 2) (a : ZMod p) :
    (rootCount p a : ℤ) = quadraticChar (ZMod p) a + 1 := by
  have hchar : ringChar (ZMod p) ≠ 2 := by
    rwa [ZMod.ringChar_zmod_n]
  simpa [rootCount] using quadraticChar_card_sqrts hchar a

/-- **Admissible primes hit twice per period.**  If `N` is a nonzero square mod
an odd prime `p`, then exactly `2` of the `p` residues `x` give `p ∣ x^2 - N`. -/
theorem root_count_of_isSquare (hp : p ≠ 2) {a : ZMod p} (ha : a ≠ 0)
    (hsq : IsSquare a) : rootCount p a = 2 := by
  have h1 : quadraticChar (ZMod p) a = 1 :=
    (quadraticChar_one_iff_isSquare ha).2 hsq
  have := rootCount_eq hp a
  rw [h1] at this
  exact_mod_cast this

/-- **Inadmissible primes never hit.**  If `N` is a non-square mod `p` then no
`x` gives `p ∣ x^2 - N`. -/
theorem root_count_of_not_isSquare (hp : p ≠ 2) {a : ZMod p} (hsq : ¬ IsSquare a) :
    rootCount p a = 0 := by
  have h1 : quadraticChar (ZMod p) a = -1 :=
    (quadraticChar_neg_one_iff_not_isSquare (F := ZMod p)).2 hsq
  have h2 : ((rootCount p a : ℕ) : ℤ) = 0 := by rw [rootCount_eq hp a, h1]; ring
  exact_mod_cast h2

/-- At `a = 0` there is exactly one root (`x = 0`): the ramified case `p ∣ N`. -/
theorem root_count_zero : rootCount p (0 : ZMod p) = 1 := by
  simp [rootCount, pow_eq_zero_iff]

/-! ## The exact cancellation -/

/-- **Total hit count over a full period of moduli.**  Summing the local hit
count over *all* residues `a` of `N` gives exactly `p`: on average, exactly one
`x` per period, which is precisely the count for a random integer sequence.
Half the moduli are excluded, and the surviving half is hit twice as often. -/
theorem expected_hits_eq_one (hp : p ≠ 2) :
    ∑ a : ZMod p, rootCount p a = p := by
  have hchar : ringChar (ZMod p) ≠ 2 := by rwa [ZMod.ringChar_zmod_n]
  have hcast : ((∑ a : ZMod p, rootCount p a : ℕ) : ℤ) = (p : ℤ) := by
    push_cast
    calc ∑ a : ZMod p, (rootCount p a : ℤ)
        = ∑ a : ZMod p, (quadraticChar (ZMod p) a + 1) := by
          exact Finset.sum_congr rfl fun a _ => rootCount_eq hp a
      _ = (∑ a : ZMod p, quadraticChar (ZMod p) a) + (Fintype.card (ZMod p) : ℤ) := by
          rw [Finset.sum_add_distrib]; simp [Finset.card_univ]
      _ = (p : ℤ) := by
          rw [quadraticChar_sum_zero hchar, ZMod.card]; ring
  exact_mod_cast hcast

/-- The admissible nonzero residues: those `a` for which some sieve value is
divisible by `p`. -/
noncomputable def admissible (p : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] : Finset (ZMod p) :=
  {a : ZMod p | a ≠ 0 ∧ IsSquare a}.toFinset

/-- **Exact cancellation: the pool is random-equivalent.**  Twice the number of
admissible nonzero residues equals the number of *all* nonzero residues.  The
factor `2` lost in prime availability (only half the primes admit a relation) is
recovered exactly by the factor `2` gained in hit density, so the expected local
valuation of a sieve value matches that of a random integer. -/
theorem relation_pool_random_equivalent (hp : p ≠ 2) :
    2 * (admissible p).card = p - 1 := by
  classical
  have hsplit :
      ∑ a : ZMod p, rootCount p a
        = rootCount p (0 : ZMod p) + ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.erase (0 : ZMod p), rootCount p a := by
    rw [← Finset.sum_erase_add _ _ (Finset.mem_univ (0 : ZMod p))]
    ring
  have hsum_erase : ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.erase (0 : ZMod p), rootCount p a = p - 1 := by
    have := expected_hits_eq_one (p := p) hp
    rw [hsplit, root_count_zero] at this
    omega
  -- on the nonzero residues the summand is `2` on `admissible` and `0` elsewhere
  have hset : (admissible p) ⊆ Finset.univ.erase (0 : ZMod p) := by
    intro a ha
    simp only [admissible, Set.mem_toFinset, Set.mem_setOf_eq] at ha
    exact Finset.mem_erase.2 ⟨ha.1, Finset.mem_univ a⟩
  have hsum_split :
      ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.erase (0 : ZMod p), rootCount p a
        = ∑ a ∈ admissible p, rootCount p a := by
    refine (Finset.sum_subset hset ?_).symm
    intro a ha hna
    have ha0 : a ≠ 0 := (Finset.mem_erase.1 ha).1
    have : ¬ IsSquare a := by
      intro hsq
      exact hna (by simp [admissible, ha0, hsq])
    exact root_count_of_not_isSquare hp this
  have hconst : ∑ a ∈ admissible p, rootCount p a = 2 * (admissible p).card := by
    rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun a ha => ?_), Finset.sum_const, smul_eq_mul,
      Nat.mul_comm]
    simp only [admissible, Set.mem_toFinset, Set.mem_setOf_eq] at ha
    exact root_count_of_isSquare hp ha.1 ha.2
  omega

/-- **Half the residues are admissible.**  Exactly `(p-1)/2` of the `p-1` nonzero
residues `N` admit a relation modulo `p`. -/
theorem card_admissible_residues (hp : p ≠ 2) :
    (admissible p).card = (p - 1) / 2 := by
  have := relation_pool_random_equivalent (p := p) hp
  omega

/-! ## Lab notes: machine-checked instances of the identities

The following finite checks are verified by the kernel (`decide`), and are the
small-scale instances of the theorems above; they reproduce, exactly, the
`hitcounts ∈ {0,1,2}`, `#admissible = (p-1)/2`, `total = p` pattern measured
numerically in `ComputationalEvidence.md` for `p = 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 31`. -/

section LabNotes

/-- `p = 7`, `N ≡ 2`: an admissible modulus is hit twice per period. -/
example : (Finset.univ.filter (fun x : ZMod 7 => x ^ 2 = 2)).card = 2 := by decide

/-- `p = 7`, `N ≡ 3`: an inadmissible modulus is never hit. -/
example : (Finset.univ.filter (fun x : ZMod 7 => x ^ 2 = 3)).card = 0 := by decide

/-- `p = 11`: exactly `(11-1)/2 = 5` nonzero admissible residues. -/
example :
    (Finset.univ.filter (fun a : ZMod 11 => a ≠ 0 ∧ ∃ x : ZMod 11, x ^ 2 = a)).card = 5 := by
  decide

/-- `p = 13`: the total hit count over a full period of moduli is `13`
(`expected_hits_eq_one`). -/
example : ∑ a : ZMod 13, (Finset.univ.filter (fun x : ZMod 13 => x ^ 2 = a)).card = 13 := by
  decide

end LabNotes

end QSRelationPool

import Mathlib
import Catalog.Shared.QSRelationPoolRandom

/-!
# Why the two factors of two cancel: they are the same `2`

`Catalog.Shared.QSRelationPoolRandom` proves the numerical cancellation that
explains the measured random-equivalence of the quadratic-sieve relation pool:
only `(p-1)/2` residues `N` admit a relation modulo `p`, but each admissible one
is hit by `2` residues `x` per period, so the expected number of hits per period
is exactly `1`, as for a random integer sequence.

This file identifies the *structural* reason.  Both factors of `2` are the order
of the kernel of the squaring endomorphism of `(ZMod p)ˣ`, i.e. the group
`{1, -1}`:

* the fibre of the squaring map is a coset of `{±1}`, which is why an admissible
  prime hits twice (`sqrt_set_eq_pair`, `rootCount_eq_card_ker`);
* the image of the squaring map has index `|{±1}| = 2`, which is why only half
  the residues are admissible (`card_ker_mul_card_admissible`).

So the "quadratic-character constraint" and the "doubled hit density" are two
faces of the single `Z/2` symmetry `x ↦ -x` of the sieve polynomial `x^2 - N`,
and their product is forced to be `1` by the orbit–stabiliser identity.  No
amount of extra scale can create a discrepancy: the cancellation is an identity,
not an asymptotic.

Main results:

* `neg_ne_self_of_ne_zero` — the `Z/2` action `x ↦ -x` on roots is free.
* `sqrt_set_eq_pair` — a fibre of squaring is exactly `{x, -x}`.
* `card_ker_sq` — the kernel of `u ↦ u^2` on `(ZMod p)ˣ` has order `2`.
* `rootCount_eq_card_ker` — the local hit count of an admissible modulus is the
  kernel order.
* `card_ker_mul_card_admissible` — kernel order times number of admissible
  residues is `|(ZMod p)ˣ|`: the exact orbit–stabiliser cancellation.
* `pool_expected_hits_eq_random` — final form: the pool's expected hit count per
  period equals the random model's, exactly, at every prime.
-/

namespace QSPoolKernel

open Finset QSRelationPool

variable {p : ℕ} [Fact p.Prime]

/-- For odd `p`, negation acts freely on the nonzero elements of `ZMod p`. -/
theorem neg_ne_self_of_ne_zero (hp : p ≠ 2) {x : ZMod p} (hx : x ≠ 0) : -x ≠ x := by
  intro h
  have h2 : (2 : ZMod p) * x = 0 := by
    have : x + x = 0 := by
      calc x + x = -x + x := by rw [h]
        _ = 0 := by ring
    linear_combination this
  rcases mul_eq_zero.1 h2 with h3 | h3
  · have hdvd : (p : ℕ) ∣ 2 := (ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff 2 p).1 (by exact_mod_cast h3)
    have hple : p ≤ 2 := Nat.le_of_dvd (by norm_num) hdvd
    have := (Fact.out (p := p.Prime)).two_le
    omega
  · exact hx h3

/-- **The fibre of squaring is a `{±1}`-coset.**  If `x^2 = a ≠ 0` then the set of
square roots of `a` is exactly `{x, -x}`, a free orbit of the `Z/2` symmetry of
the sieve polynomial. -/
theorem sqrt_set_eq_pair {a x : ZMod p} (hx : x ^ 2 = a) :
    {y : ZMod p | y ^ 2 = a} = {x, -x} := by
  ext y
  simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq, Set.mem_insert_iff, Set.mem_singleton_iff]
  constructor
  · intro hy
    have h : (y - x) * (y + x) = 0 := by
      have : y ^ 2 - x ^ 2 = 0 := by rw [hy, hx]; ring
      linear_combination this
    rcases mul_eq_zero.1 h with h1 | h1
    · left; linear_combination h1
    · right; linear_combination h1
  · rintro (rfl | rfl)
    · exact hx
    · rw [← hx]; ring

/-- The squaring endomorphism of the unit group. -/
noncomputable def sqUnits (p : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] : (ZMod p)ˣ →* (ZMod p)ˣ :=
  powMonoidHom 2

theorem mem_ker_sqUnits_iff {u : (ZMod p)ˣ} :
    u ∈ MonoidHom.ker (sqUnits p) ↔ u = 1 ∨ u = -1 := by
  constructor
  · intro hu
    have hu' : (u : ZMod p) ^ 2 = 1 := by
      have := MonoidHom.mem_ker.1 hu
      simpa [sqUnits, powMonoidHom] using congrArg (fun v : (ZMod p)ˣ => (v : ZMod p)) this
    have h : ((u : ZMod p) - 1) * ((u : ZMod p) + 1) = 0 := by linear_combination hu'
    rcases mul_eq_zero.1 h with h1 | h1
    · left
      apply Units.ext
      have : (u : ZMod p) = 1 := by linear_combination h1
      simpa using this
    · right
      apply Units.ext
      have : (u : ZMod p) = -1 := by linear_combination h1
      simpa using this
  · rintro (rfl | rfl) <;> simp [MonoidHom.mem_ker, sqUnits, powMonoidHom]

/-- **The kernel of squaring has order `2`** for odd `p`: it is `{1, -1}`. -/
theorem card_ker_sqUnits (hp : p ≠ 2) :
    Nat.card (MonoidHom.ker (sqUnits p)) = 2 := by
  have hcoe : ((MonoidHom.ker (sqUnits p) : Subgroup (ZMod p)ˣ) : Set (ZMod p)ˣ)
      = {1, -1} := by
    ext u
    simpa using mem_ker_sqUnits_iff (p := p) (u := u)
  have hp2 : 2 < p := lt_of_le_of_ne (Fact.out (p := p.Prime)).two_le (Ne.symm hp)
  haveI : Fact (2 < p) := ⟨hp2⟩
  have hne : (1 : (ZMod p)ˣ) ≠ -1 := by
    intro h
    have h1 : (1 : ZMod p) = -1 := by
      simpa using congrArg (fun v : (ZMod p)ˣ => (v : ZMod p)) h
    exact (ZMod.neg_one_ne_one (n := p)) h1.symm
  calc Nat.card (MonoidHom.ker (sqUnits p))
      = Nat.card ({1, -1} : Set (ZMod p)ˣ) := Nat.card_congr (Equiv.setCongr hcoe)
    _ = 2 := by rw [Nat.card_coe_set_eq, Set.ncard_pair hne]

/-- **The local hit count of an admissible modulus is the kernel order.** -/
theorem rootCount_eq_card_ker (hp : p ≠ 2) {a : ZMod p} (ha : a ≠ 0)
    (hsq : IsSquare a) :
    rootCount p a = Nat.card (MonoidHom.ker (sqUnits p)) := by
  rw [card_ker_sqUnits hp, root_count_of_isSquare hp ha hsq]

/-- **Orbit–stabiliser cancellation.**  The order of the kernel `{±1}` times the
number of admissible residues is the order of the whole unit group: the factor
`2` lost by the quadratic-character constraint is *the same* `2` gained by the
doubled hit density. -/
theorem card_ker_mul_card_admissible (hp : p ≠ 2) :
    Nat.card (MonoidHom.ker (sqUnits p)) * (admissible p).card
      = Fintype.card (ZMod p)ˣ := by
  have hcards : Fintype.card (ZMod p)ˣ = p - 1 := by
    rw [ZMod.card_units_eq_totient, Nat.totient_prime (Fact.out (p := p.Prime))]
  rw [card_ker_sqUnits hp, hcards]
  exact relation_pool_random_equivalent hp

/-- **Final form.**  Averaged over the residue of `N`, the number of `x` per
period with `p ∣ x^2 - N` is exactly `1`, the value for a random integer
sequence: the quadratic-sieve relation pool is random-equivalent at every prime,
exactly, with no error term to shrink with scale. -/
theorem pool_expected_hits_eq_random (hp : p ≠ 2) :
    ∑ a : ZMod p, rootCount p a = Fintype.card (ZMod p) := by
  rw [ZMod.card]
  exact expected_hits_eq_one hp

end QSPoolKernel

import Mathlib
import Catalog.Shared.QSRelationPoolRandom

/-!
# Universality of on-average random-equivalence for sieve polynomials

The exact cancellation of `Catalog.Shared.QSRelationPoolRandom` invites the
question: is the quadratic sieve special?  It is not.  This file isolates the
combinatorial skeleton of the phenomenon and shows it is *universal*: for **any**
sieve map `f` on residues (any polynomial, any degree, any modulus), the number
of `x` per period hitting a given target residue averages to exactly
`|domain| / |targets|`, the random-model value.  Averaged over the target, no
sieve polynomial can be better or worse than random.

What the individual polynomial controls is only the *distribution* of that hit
count across targets, and the file characterises exactly when the pool is
random-equivalent target-by-target rather than merely on average:

* `sum_fiber_card` — the averaging identity (universality).
* `pointwise_uniform_iff_bijective` — pointwise random-equivalence holds iff the
  sieve map is a bijection of residues.
* `sq_not_pointwise_uniform` — for `x ↦ x^2` mod an odd prime it fails: the
  hit count is the `2`/`0` dichotomy, never the constant `1`.
* `qs_average_hits_eq_random` — but on average over the modulus residue the
  quadratic sieve hits exactly once per period, like a random sequence.

The moral for the experiment: any measured deviation of the `x^2 - N` pool from
the random control must come from the *interaction across primes* for one fixed
`N`, never from the one-prime statistics, which are pinned by these identities.
-/

namespace SieveUniversality

open Finset

variable {α β : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype β] [DecidableEq β]

/-- The number of `x` in one period which the sieve map `f` sends to `b`. -/
def hitCount (f : α → β) (b : β) : ℕ := (Finset.univ.filter (fun x => f x = b)).card

/-- **Universality of the average hit count.**  Whatever the sieve map, the hit
counts sum to the size of one period; the mean hit count per target is exactly
`|α| / |β|`, the random-model prediction. -/
theorem sum_fiber_card (f : α → β) :
    ∑ b : β, hitCount f b = Fintype.card α := by
  have h := Finset.card_eq_sum_card_fiberwise
      (f := f) (s := (Finset.univ : Finset α)) (t := (Finset.univ : Finset β))
      (fun x _ => Finset.mem_univ (f x))
  simp only [hitCount, Fintype.card]
  exact h.symm

omit [Fintype β] in
/-- **Pointwise random-equivalence is exactly bijectivity.**  A sieve map hits
every target exactly once per period iff it is a bijection of residues; any
non-bijective sieve map (such as squaring) necessarily has a nontrivial
`0`/`≥2` dichotomy, which is what a quadratic-character constraint looks like. -/
theorem pointwise_uniform_iff_bijective (f : α → β) :
    (∀ b, hitCount f b = 1) ↔ Function.Bijective f := by
  classical
  constructor
  · intro h
    constructor
    · intro x y hxy
      have hcard : (Finset.univ.filter (fun z => f z = f x)).card = 1 := h (f x)
      obtain ⟨z, hz⟩ := Finset.card_eq_one.1 hcard
      have hx : x ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun z => f z = f x) := by simp
      have hy : y ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun z => f z = f x) := by simp [hxy]
      rw [hz] at hx hy
      simp only [Finset.mem_singleton] at hx hy
      rw [hx, hy]
    · intro b
      have hcard : (Finset.univ.filter (fun z => f z = b)).card = 1 := h b
      obtain ⟨z, hz⟩ := Finset.card_eq_one.1 hcard
      have : z ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun w => f w = b) := by rw [hz]; simp
      exact ⟨z, (Finset.mem_filter.1 this).2⟩
  · rintro ⟨hinj, hsurj⟩ b
    obtain ⟨a, rfl⟩ := hsurj b
    have : Finset.univ.filter (fun z => f z = f a) = {a} := by
      ext z
      simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_univ, true_and, Finset.mem_singleton]
      exact ⟨fun h => hinj h, fun h => by rw [h]⟩
    rw [hitCount, this, Finset.card_singleton]

/-! ## The quadratic sieve instance -/

variable {p : ℕ} [Fact p.Prime]

theorem hitCount_eq_rootCount (a : ZMod p) :
    hitCount (fun x : ZMod p => x ^ 2) a = QSRelationPool.rootCount p a := by
  classical
  simp [hitCount, QSRelationPool.rootCount, Set.toFinset_setOf]

/-- **The quadratic sieve is not pointwise random.**  Squaring mod an odd prime
is not a bijection, so the per-modulus hit count is never identically `1`: half
the residues are missed and the other half are hit twice. -/
theorem sq_not_pointwise_uniform (hp : p ≠ 2) :
    ¬ (∀ a : ZMod p, hitCount (fun x : ZMod p => x ^ 2) a = 1) := by
  intro h
  have hbij : Function.Bijective (fun x : ZMod p => x ^ 2) :=
    (pointwise_uniform_iff_bijective _).1 h
  have hp2 : 2 < p := lt_of_le_of_ne (Fact.out (p := p.Prime)).two_le (Ne.symm hp)
  haveI : Fact (2 < p) := ⟨hp2⟩
  have hne : (-1 : ZMod p) ≠ 1 := ZMod.neg_one_ne_one
  exact hne (hbij.1 (by ring))

/-- **But it is random on average.**  Averaged over the residue of `N`, the
quadratic-sieve map hits exactly once per period — the random-model value. -/
theorem qs_average_hits_eq_random (hp : p ≠ 2) :
    ∑ a : ZMod p, hitCount (fun x : ZMod p => x ^ 2) a = Fintype.card (ZMod p) := by
  rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun a _ => hitCount_eq_rootCount a), ZMod.card]
  exact QSRelationPool.expected_hits_eq_one hp

end SieveUniversality

import Mathlib
import Catalog.Shared.NumberTheory.IsSmooth

/-!
# Rigorous sparsity of the smooth pool, from the exponent-vector injection

Context (experiment 465, paper 130).  The quadratic sieve needs `B`-smooth values
`x^2 - N`; the whole subexponential run time is a trade-off between the *size* of
the factor base (`π(B)` relations must be collected) and the *rarity* of smooth
values.  Everything asymptotic about that trade-off is Dickman heuristics; this
file records the part that is an unconditional theorem, and which is the true
reason the smooth pool is thin at fixed `B`:

> a `B`-smooth number `n ≤ x` is *determined* by its exponent vector, whose
> entries are at most `log₂ x`, so there are at most `(log₂ x + 1) ^ π(B)` of
> them — polylogarithmic in `x` for fixed `B`.

This is the finite, unconditional skeleton underneath the `ρ(u)` model: it forces
`B → ∞` with `x`, which is what makes the sieve subexponential rather than
polynomial.  It is proved here by an explicit injection of the smooth pool into
the space of exponent vectors, using the catalog predicate `isSmooth` of
`Catalog.Shared.NumberTheory.IsSmooth`.

Main results:

* `mem_smoothPool_iff` — the decidable pool predicate agrees with the catalog
  predicate `isSmooth`.
* `factorization_le_log_two` — every exponent of a number `≤ x` is `≤ log₂ x`.
* `smoothPool_card_le` — `Ψ(x,B) ≤ (log₂ x + 1) ^ π(B)`.
* `smoothPool_card_le_pow_pi` — the same bound with the factor base written as
  the prime-counting function.
* `smoothPool_one` — the extreme case `B = 1`: only `n = 1` is `1`-smooth.
-/

namespace SmoothSparsity

open Finset

/-- The factor base: primes `p ≤ B`. -/
def factorBase (B : ℕ) : Finset ℕ := (Finset.range (B + 1)).filter Nat.Prime

/-- The smooth pool `Ψ(x,B)` as a finset: the `B`-smooth integers in `[1, x]`. -/
def smoothPool (B x : ℕ) : Finset ℕ :=
  (Finset.Icc 1 x).filter (fun n => ∀ p ∈ n.primeFactors, p ≤ B)

theorem mem_factorBase {B p : ℕ} : p ∈ factorBase B ↔ p.Prime ∧ p ≤ B := by
  simp [factorBase, and_comm]

/-- The decidable pool predicate is the catalog predicate `isSmooth`, on positive
integers. -/
theorem mem_smoothPool_iff {B x n : ℕ} (hn : n ≠ 0) :
    n ∈ smoothPool B x ↔ (1 ≤ n ∧ n ≤ x) ∧ isSmooth B n := by
  simp only [smoothPool, Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_Icc, isSmooth,
    Nat.mem_primeFactors]
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨h1, h2⟩
    exact ⟨h1, fun p hp hpd => h2 p ⟨hp, hpd, hn⟩⟩
  · rintro ⟨h1, h2⟩
    exact ⟨h1, fun p hp => h2 p hp.1 hp.2.1⟩

/-- Only the primes of the factor base occur in a pooled number. -/
theorem primeFactors_subset {B x n : ℕ} (hn : n ∈ smoothPool B x) :
    n.primeFactors ⊆ factorBase B := by
  intro p hp
  have h := (Finset.mem_filter.1 hn).2 p hp
  exact mem_factorBase.2 ⟨Nat.prime_of_mem_primeFactors hp, h⟩

/-- **Every exponent is small.**  If `0 < n ≤ x` then each exponent in the prime
factorisation of `n` is at most `log₂ x`. -/
theorem factorization_le_log_two {x n p : ℕ} (hn : n ≠ 0) (hx : n ≤ x) :
    n.factorization p ≤ Nat.log 2 x := by
  rcases eq_or_ne (n.factorization p) 0 with h | h
  · simp [h]
  have hmem : p ∈ n.primeFactors := by
    rw [← Nat.support_factorization]
    exact Finsupp.mem_support_iff.2 h
  have hp : p.Prime := Nat.prime_of_mem_primeFactors hmem
  have hx0 : x ≠ 0 := by rintro rfl; omega
  have hdvd : p ^ n.factorization p ∣ n := Nat.ordProj_dvd n p
  have hple : p ^ n.factorization p ≤ n := Nat.le_of_dvd (Nat.pos_of_ne_zero hn) hdvd
  have h2 : 2 ^ n.factorization p ≤ p ^ n.factorization p :=
    Nat.pow_le_pow_left hp.two_le _
  exact (Nat.le_log_iff_pow_le (by norm_num) hx0).2 (le_trans h2 (le_trans hple hx))
/-- **Sparsity of the smooth pool.**  There are at most `(log₂ x + 1) ^ π(B)`
`B`-smooth numbers in `[1, x]`: for a fixed factor base the pool grows only
polylogarithmically in `x`. -/
theorem smoothPool_card_le (B x : ℕ) :
    (smoothPool B x).card ≤ (Nat.log 2 x + 1) ^ (factorBase B).card := by
  classical
  set k := Nat.log 2 x with hk
  -- the exponent-vector map
  set f : ℕ → (factorBase B → Fin (k + 1)) :=
    fun n p => ⟨min (n.factorization p) k, by omega⟩ with hf
  have hcard : Fintype.card (factorBase B → Fin (k + 1)) = (k + 1) ^ (factorBase B).card := by
    simp
  have hinj : Set.InjOn f (smoothPool B x) := by
    intro a ha b hb hab
    simp only [Finset.mem_coe, smoothPool, Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_Icc] at ha hb
    have ha0 : a ≠ 0 := by omega
    have hb0 : b ≠ 0 := by omega
    have hfa : ∀ p, a.factorization p = b.factorization p := by
      intro p
      by_cases hp : p ∈ factorBase B
      · have := congrFun hab ⟨p, hp⟩
        simp only [hf, Fin.mk.injEq] at this
        have h1 : a.factorization p ≤ k :=
          factorization_le_log_two ha0 ha.1.2
        have h2 : b.factorization p ≤ k :=
          factorization_le_log_two hb0 hb.1.2
        omega
      · have hA : a.factorization p = 0 := by
          by_contra hcon
          have hmem : p ∈ a.primeFactors := by
            rw [← Nat.support_factorization]
            exact Finsupp.mem_support_iff.2 hcon
          exact hp (mem_factorBase.2
            ⟨Nat.prime_of_mem_primeFactors hmem, ha.2 p hmem⟩)
        have hB : b.factorization p = 0 := by
          by_contra hcon
          have hmem : p ∈ b.primeFactors := by
            rw [← Nat.support_factorization]
            exact Finsupp.mem_support_iff.2 hcon
          exact hp (mem_factorBase.2
            ⟨Nat.prime_of_mem_primeFactors hmem, hb.2 p hmem⟩)
        rw [hA, hB]
    have : a.factorization = b.factorization := Finsupp.ext hfa
    exact Nat.factorization_inj (Set.mem_setOf_eq ▸ ha0) (Set.mem_setOf_eq ▸ hb0) this
  calc (smoothPool B x).card
      ≤ (Finset.univ : Finset (factorBase B → Fin (k + 1))).card :=
        Finset.card_le_card_of_injOn f (fun n _ => Finset.mem_univ _) hinj
    _ = (k + 1) ^ (factorBase B).card := by rw [← hcard]; rfl

/-- The same bound with the factor base size written as `π(B)`, the number of
primes up to `B`. -/
theorem smoothPool_card_le_pow_pi (B x : ℕ) :
    (smoothPool B x).card ≤ (Nat.log 2 x + 1) ^ ((Finset.range (B + 1)).filter Nat.Prime).card :=
  smoothPool_card_le B x

/-- The extreme case: with an empty factor base (`B = 1`) the pool is `{1}`. -/
theorem smoothPool_one (x : ℕ) (hx : 1 ≤ x) : smoothPool 1 x = {1} := by
  ext n
  simp only [smoothPool, Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_Icc, Finset.mem_singleton]
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨⟨h1, h2⟩, h3⟩
    by_contra hne
    have hn : 2 ≤ n := by omega
    obtain ⟨p, hp, hpd⟩ := Nat.exists_prime_and_dvd (n := n) (by omega)
    have hmem : p ∈ n.primeFactors := Nat.mem_primeFactors.2 ⟨hp, hpd, by omega⟩
    have := h3 p hmem
    have := hp.two_le
    omega
  · rintro rfl
    simp [hx]

end SmoothSparsity

import Mathlib
import Catalog.Shared.QSRelationPoolRandom
import Catalog.Shared.SmoothCountSparsity

/-!
# The factor base the relations actually live in, and the `𝔽₂` dimension bound

The measurements of experiment 465 say that the *input statistics* of the
quadratic sieve are those of a random pool.  What is then left as the sieve's
genuine advantage is algorithmic, and this file formalises the two algebraic
facts that constitute it.

1. **The support of a relation is confined to the admissible primes.**  A
   `B`-smooth value `x^2 - N` factors only over primes `p ≤ B` for which `N` is a
   quadratic residue (`smooth_qsValue_support`).  So the exponent vectors of the
   relations do not live in `𝔽₂^{π(B)}` but in the much smaller subspace indexed
   by the admissible primes.

2. **A dimension count then produces a congruence of squares.**  Any family of
   more nonzero naturals than the size of their common support admits a nonempty
   sub-family whose product is a perfect square
   (`exists_nonempty_subset_prod_isSquare`), because their `𝔽₂` exponent vectors
   must be linearly dependent.

Combining the two gives `qs_congruence_of_squares`: `|A| + 1` smooth sieve values
suffice to build a square, where `A` is the set of *admissible* primes — half the
factor base — rather than the whole factor base.  This is the precise sense in
which the quadratic-character constraint, which costs nothing in smoothness
probability (see `Catalog.Shared.QSRelationPoolRandom`), is a *gain* in the
linear-algebra stage.

Main results:

* `isSquare_of_even_factorization` — even exponents means perfect square.
* `exists_nonempty_subset_prod_isSquare` — the `𝔽₂` dependency argument.
* `smooth_qsValue_support` — relations are supported on admissible primes.
* `qs_congruence_of_squares` — end-to-end: `|A| + 1` relations give a square.
-/

namespace QSDimension

open Finset

/-- A nonzero natural with all exponents even is a perfect square. -/
theorem isSquare_of_even_factorization {n : ℕ} (hn : n ≠ 0)
    (h : ∀ p, Even (n.factorization p)) : IsSquare n := by
  classical
  refine ⟨∏ p ∈ n.factorization.support, p ^ (n.factorization p / 2), ?_⟩
  have hself : ∏ p ∈ n.factorization.support, p ^ (n.factorization p) = n := by
    simpa [Finsupp.prod] using Nat.factorization_prod_pow_eq_self hn
  have hstep : ∏ p ∈ n.factorization.support,
      (p ^ (n.factorization p / 2) * p ^ (n.factorization p / 2))
      = ∏ p ∈ n.factorization.support, p ^ (n.factorization p) := by
    refine Finset.prod_congr rfl (fun p _ => ?_)
    rw [← pow_add]
    congr 1
    obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := h p
    omega
  rw [← Finset.prod_mul_distrib, hstep, hself]

/-- **The dimension bound behind the sieve's linear-algebra step.**  If more than
`S.card` nonzero naturals all factor over the prime set `S`, then some nonempty
sub-family has a perfect-square product: their `𝔽₂`-exponent vectors live in a
space of dimension `S.card` and must be dependent. -/
theorem exists_nonempty_subset_prod_isSquare {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (S : Finset ℕ) (v : ι → ℕ) (hv : ∀ i, v i ≠ 0)
    (hsupp : ∀ i, ∀ p, (v i).factorization p ≠ 0 → p ∈ S)
    (hcard : S.card < Fintype.card ι) :
    ∃ T : Finset ι, T.Nonempty ∧ IsSquare (∏ i ∈ T, v i) := by
  classical
  set w : ι → (S → ZMod 2) := fun i p => (((v i).factorization p : ℕ) : ZMod 2) with hw
  have hnli : ¬ LinearIndependent (ZMod 2) w := by
    intro hli
    have hb := hli.fintype_card_le_finrank
    rw [Module.finrank_fintype_fun_eq_card, Fintype.card_coe] at hb
    omega
  obtain ⟨g, hgsum, i₀, hi₀⟩ := Fintype.not_linearIndependent_iff.1 hnli
  set T : Finset ι := Finset.univ.filter (fun i => g i ≠ 0) with hT
  have hTne : T.Nonempty := ⟨i₀, by simp [hT, hi₀]⟩
  have hg1 : ∀ i ∈ T, g i = 1 := by
    intro i hi
    have : g i ≠ 0 := (Finset.mem_filter.1 hi).2
    revert this
    generalize g i = a
    revert a
    decide
  have hprod_ne : (∏ i ∈ T, v i) ≠ 0 := by
    refine Finset.prod_ne_zero_iff.2 (fun i _ => hv i)
  refine ⟨T, hTne, isSquare_of_even_factorization hprod_ne (fun p => ?_)⟩
  have hfact : (∏ i ∈ T, v i).factorization p = ∑ i ∈ T, (v i).factorization p := by
    rw [Nat.factorization_prod (fun i _ => hv i)]
    simp
  by_cases hpS : p ∈ S
  · -- use the `𝔽₂` dependency at the coordinate `p`
    have hzero : ∑ i : ι, g i * w i ⟨p, hpS⟩ = 0 := by
      have h := congrFun hgsum ⟨p, hpS⟩
      simpa [Finset.sum_apply, Pi.smul_apply, smul_eq_mul] using h
    have hzeroout : ∀ i ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset ι), i ∉ T → g i * w i ⟨p, hpS⟩ = 0 := by
      intro i _ hiT
      have hgi : g i = 0 := by
        by_contra hc
        exact hiT (Finset.mem_filter.2 ⟨Finset.mem_univ i, hc⟩)
      simp [hgi]
    have hsub : ∑ i ∈ T, (g i * w i ⟨p, hpS⟩) = ∑ i : ι, g i * w i ⟨p, hpS⟩ :=
      Finset.sum_subset (Finset.filter_subset _ _) hzeroout
    have hone : ∑ i ∈ T, (g i * w i ⟨p, hpS⟩) = ∑ i ∈ T, w i ⟨p, hpS⟩ :=
      Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun i hi => by rw [hg1 i hi, one_mul])
    have hsum0 : ((∑ i ∈ T, (v i).factorization p : ℕ) : ZMod 2) = 0 := by
      have : ∑ i ∈ T, w i ⟨p, hpS⟩ = 0 := by rw [← hone, hsub, hzero]
      simpa [hw] using this
    rw [hfact, even_iff_two_dvd, ← ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff]
    exact hsum0
  · have : ∀ i ∈ T, (v i).factorization p = 0 := by
      intro i _
      by_contra hcon
      exact hpS (hsupp i p hcon)
    rw [hfact, Finset.sum_congr rfl this]
    simp

/-! ## The quadratic-sieve specialisation -/

open Classical in
/-- The *admissible* part of the factor base for the modulus `N`: the primes
`p ≤ B` for which `N` is a quadratic residue.  Only these can occur in a
relation. -/
noncomputable def admissiblePrimes (N : ℤ) (B : ℕ) : Finset ℕ :=
  (SmoothSparsity.factorBase B).filter (fun p => IsSquare ((N : ZMod p)))

theorem admissiblePrimes_subset (N : ℤ) (B : ℕ) :
    admissiblePrimes N B ⊆ SmoothSparsity.factorBase B := by
  classical
  simp [admissiblePrimes, Finset.filter_subset]

/-- **Relations are supported on admissible primes.**  Every prime occurring in a
`B`-smooth sieve value `x^2 - N` lies in the admissible half of the factor
base. -/
theorem smooth_qsValue_support {B : ℕ} {N x : ℤ} {v : ℕ}
    (hval : (v : ℤ) = x ^ 2 - N)
    (hsm : ∀ p ∈ v.primeFactors, p ≤ B) :
    ∀ p, v.factorization p ≠ 0 → p ∈ admissiblePrimes N B := by
  classical
  intro p hp
  have hmem : p ∈ v.primeFactors := by
    rw [← Nat.support_factorization]
    exact Finsupp.mem_support_iff.2 hp
  have hprime : p.Prime := Nat.prime_of_mem_primeFactors hmem
  have hdvdn : p ∣ v := Nat.dvd_of_mem_primeFactors hmem
  have hdvd : (p : ℤ) ∣ QSRelationPool.qsValue N x := by
    rw [QSRelationPool.qsValue, ← hval]
    exact_mod_cast Int.natCast_dvd_natCast.2 hdvdn
  have hsq : IsSquare ((N : ZMod p)) := QSRelationPool.isSquare_of_dvd_qsValue hdvd
  refine Finset.mem_filter.2 ⟨SmoothSparsity.mem_factorBase.2 ⟨hprime, hsm p hmem⟩, hsq⟩

/-- **End-to-end: a congruence of squares from `|A| + 1` relations.**  Given more
`B`-smooth sieve values `x^2 - N` than there are *admissible* primes, some
nonempty subproduct of them is a perfect square.  The bound involves only the
admissible half of the factor base — the quadratic-character constraint, which
costs nothing in smoothness probability, halves the number of relations that must
be collected. -/
theorem qs_congruence_of_squares {B : ℕ} {N : ℤ} {n : ℕ} (X : Fin n → ℤ) (V : Fin n → ℕ)
    (hV0 : ∀ i, V i ≠ 0) (hval : ∀ i, (V i : ℤ) = (X i) ^ 2 - N)
    (hsm : ∀ i, ∀ p ∈ (V i).primeFactors, p ≤ B)
    (hcard : (admissiblePrimes N B).card < n) :
    ∃ T : Finset (Fin n), T.Nonempty ∧ IsSquare (∏ i ∈ T, V i) := by
  classical
  refine exists_nonempty_subset_prod_isSquare (admissiblePrimes N B) V hV0 ?_ ?_
  · intro i p hp
    exact smooth_qsValue_support (hval i) (hsm i) p hp
  · simpa using hcard

end QSDimension
